- Good evening, my name is Angie Rogers,
and I live in Coralville.
I'm here tonight to speak about
the proposed '26-'27 budget reductions
and specifically the priorities reflected

in the proposal presented
by administration.

I understand the district
must reduce spending
by at least $6 million.

I do not minimize the
difficulty of this reality,

and I understand that no set
of reductions will be painless.

But what concerns me is not
simply that cuts are being made.

What concerns me is where
they are being made first
and how they are being justified.
When we review the proposed reductions,

the most concrete and
clearly identified cuts
are overwhelmingly student-facing.
Elementary classroom teachers, $900,000.
Middle school staff, $500,000.
High school staff, $600,000.

Non-renewal of selected
probationary teachers, $1 million.
Pre-K through 12 support staff, $600,000.

Special education, lead
support positions, $360,000.
Building substitutes, $200,000.

Reduction or elimination of
attendance support busing,
700,000 to $1 million.

That is approximately $5
million in identified cuts

directly affecting
classrooms, instruction,
and student support.
By contrast, administrative reductions
are described as approximately $2 million,

but those reductions
appear far less specific

and largely contingent on
reassignment or attrition.
That is not the same level of sacrifice.

Students and teachers will
feel these cuts immediately.
Central administration will not.

If this district is facing
true financial problems,

then we must be willing to
consider structural changes
at every level of the district,
including central office administration.
The core mission of a school district
is to educate students.

That means the areas cut
last should be the ones
that directly impact the mission.
Non-student-facing administrative costs
should be prioritized for reduction first.
There are many options.

There could be pay cuts
for the executive cabinet.
There could also be restructuring
and consolidation of leadership roles.
In the short term, we could also outsource
and have fractional positions for HR, CFO,
and even the superintendent.

These changes would have no
immediate impact on classrooms.

and increase class sizes,
why are we not publicly presenting
a full central office organizational chart
and compensation breakdown.
Before reducing special education support,
why aren't all consulting contracts frozen
except for legal and tax?

Before asking teachers to
ration copy paper and toner,
why are top administrative perks,

including car allowances,
cell phone allowances,

internet allowances, and
other contractual benefits,

not being reviewed or even
voluntarily suspended?
These are not symbolic questions.
They are governance questions.
They are priority questions.
And they go directly to public trust.
Families are watching. Staff are watching.

Taxpayers are watching.
Budgets reflect values.

Budgets reveal what an
institution chooses to protect
and what it chooses not to.

If classrooms absorb the
majority of reductions

while central administration
remains insulated,
that sends a clear message
and is not one that builds confidence
in district leadership or this board.
I am asking each board member
to take a hard look at the proposed cuts
and reconsider the priorities.
Protect classrooms first.

Exhaust central administration
restructuring options.

and benefit freezes at the top

before implementing permanent
classroom reductions.
Apply the same standard of transparency
to central administration

that is applied to teachers
and building staff.
Our students should not be

the district's primary
budget balancing tool.
